analysis.one_liner: Forces medical malpractice claims into binding arbitration and caps compensation for patients in federally funded care.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Senator Domenici with five Republican cosponsors, the bill got one subcommittee hearing and never reached a Senate vote before the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have taken almost every medical malpractice dispute out of court. Anyone whose care was paid for with federal money — Medicare, Medicaid, VA, public health programs — would be automatically bound to a private arbitration system, with decisions final and almost no right to appeal. Damages for pain and suffering would be capped at $250,000, awards would be reduced by any insurance payments the patient already received, and punitive damages would go to the state instead of the injured patient. It would also change the tax code so employers only get their health plan deduction if employees are locked into the same arbitration system.
analysis.who_benefits: Doctors, hospitals, and medical malpractice insurers. Arbitration with capped damages and no jury trials would mean smaller and more predictable payouts for malpractice claims, and the bill's stated goal was to cut malpractice premiums and defensive medicine costs [S2] [S3]. The new certified arbitration services would also gain, becoming the mandatory, exclusive channel for these claims [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill said only 1 in 16 people injured by medical negligence ever get compensated under the current malpractice system, and less than half of malpractice insurance premiums reach injured patients, so it aimed to replace jury trials with faster arbitration panels that must issue a written decision within six months [S3].

It capped noneconomic damages (pain and suffering) at $250,000 and barred punitive damages from going to the injured patient, which would make malpractice payouts smaller and more predictable for providers and their insurers [S3].

It allowed liability to be judged against federally certified medical practice guidelines rather than a jury's view of state standards of care, which the bill argued would reduce defensive medicine and malpractice premiums [S3].
By denying employers the business tax deduction for health plans unless employees agreed to binding arbitration, it extended the same system to workers with job-based insurance [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Patients injured by medical negligence. They would lose the right to a jury trial, lose appeal rights except for fraud or arbitrator misconduct, see awards for pain and suffering capped at $250,000, see awards reduced by any insurance they received, and see punitive damages paid to the state instead of to them [S3]. Workers in employer plans would be bound to arbitration as a condition of their employer keeping the tax deduction [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Patients injured by malpractice and their families

drawbacks.text: A patient's 'agreement' to arbitration is deemed to exist simply because their care was paid for with federal funds — there is no actual consent and no opt-out — and the arbitration decision is final with court review allowed only for corruption, fraud, arbitrator bias, or misconduct [S3].
The bill makes these procedures exclusive: no malpractice lawsuit could be filed in any state or federal court except as the bill allows [S2] [S3].

Awards would be cut twice over: noneconomic damages capped at $250,000 and any award reduced by collateral source payments such as the patient's own health insurance, meaning the patient's insurer effectively subsidizes the negligent provider's payout [S3].

The bill's own findings concede the current system fails injured patients, but its remedy restricts compensation further while making the alternative — certified no-fault compensation — optional for providers rather than guaranteed for patients [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real problem it documented itself: few injured patients ever collect, and administrative costs are high [S3]. But its remedy took away patients' court rights and capped their compensation while handing providers and insurers lower, predictable payouts; the promised cost savings would flow mainly to providers and malpractice insurers, and patients had no genuine choice to opt out. Even on its own terms, the bill guaranteed faster arbitration but not better or more complete compensation for the people it described as systematically shortchanged.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, held one subcommittee hearing in October 1991, and was never reported out of committee or voted on before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Senator Pete Domenici introduced the bill on June 6, 1991, joined by five Republican cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S1] [S3] [S5].
The Senate Finance Committee's Subcommittee on Medicare and Long-Term Care held hearings on October 18, 1991 [S5].
No further action was taken: the committee never voted the bill out, the Senate never debated it, and it died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patients injured by medical negligence kept full access to the courts and uncapped jury awards, because the bill never advanced; providers and malpractice insurers gained nothing from it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured patients, who kept their right to sue

for.name: Sen. Pete Domenici
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate on June 6, 1991.

for.name: Sens. Danforth, Rudman, Chafee, and Gramm
American Medical Association and physician groups
for.what_they_did: Backed malpractice liability restrictions including damage caps and alternatives to jury trials during the early-1990s malpractice reform debate.

against.name: Sen. Lloyd Bentsen
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or vote on the bill after it was referred to Finance; the committee took no action beyond a subcommittee hearing.

against.name: Trial lawyers and patient advocacy groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed malpractice measures that cap damages and replace jury trials with mandatory arbitration.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken. All six sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill died in a committee chaired by a Democrat, but the record shows no partisan floor fight.

industries.note: Capped noneconomic damages, reduced awards for insurance the patient already received, and no-fault arbitration would sharply lower and stabilize insurer payouts. The savings come directly out of compensation for injured patients [S3].

The bill would cut malpractice premiums and limit liability exposure, including by allowing federally certified practice guidelines to replace state standards of care. Providers would benefit at the direct expense of what injured patients could recover, though the bill argued lower premiums and less defensive medicine would also help patients [S3].

The bill makes certified private arbitration services the exclusive, mandatory forum for malpractice claims covering nearly all federally funded and employer-provided care, with final decisions and almost no court review. It creates a permanent government-certified channel replacing the public court system [S2] [S3].
Employers would keep their health plan tax deduction only by binding employees to mandatory arbitration of medical injury claims, shifting dispute costs away from plans and onto injured workers [S3].
